This relatively light body mass is typical of aerial insectivores, which must remain agile during sustained foraging flights over grasslands and savannas. Adult body mass appears to be influenced by migratory status, with individuals from southern populations that undertake longer migrations often arriving at breeding grounds with higher mass reserves. The species exhibits a modest sexual size dimorphism, with females generally falling in the lower portion of the mass range while males average slightly heavier, though the difference is not statistically significant in most studies. Comparative data from congeners suggest that Tyrannus savana is intermediate in body size within the genus, smaller than the large Scissor-tailed Flycatcher but larger than the diminutive Loggerhead Kingbird.

However, field studies employing mark-recapture methods in South American populations have documented individuals reaching over a decade of age, suggesting that this value is biologically plausible. Longevity in migratory flycatchers is often constrained by the perils of migration, including adverse weather, habitat fragmentation, and predation during stopovers. The species' life history strategy, characterized by a single annual brood and relatively low fecundity, selects for increased adult survival to maintain population stability. Senescence in this species appears gradual, with older individuals showing a decline in feather quality and reduced reproductive output in their later years, though examples of birds breeding successfully at over eight years of age have been documented in long-term study sites in Argentina.

The migration ecology of the Fork-tailed flycatcher is among the most remarkable of any passerine, with southern populations undertaking annual journeys from temperate South America to the Amazon basin and beyond. Young birds hatched in the austral spring must complete their post-fledging development and accumulate sufficient fat reserves before embarking on this demanding migration. The species is a classic aerial hawker, capturing insects in flight with acrobatic maneuvers aided by its long tail, which functions as an aerodynamic rudder. During the non-breeding season, Tyrannus savana forms large communal roosts in the Amazon lowlands, sometimes numbering thousands of individuals, a behavior that likely facilitates information sharing about optimal foraging locations. The species has also demonstrated a remarkable ability to adapt to anthropogenic landscapes, frequently nesting in roadside trees and pasturelands across its extensive range from Panama to central Argentina, though populations in the northernmost parts of the range are largely resident rather than migratory. Conservation status remains Least Concern, though local declines have been noted in areas of intensive agricultural conversion.
